parts.title: Passage — The Line We Share

parts.markdown:
> **How to do the listening.** The same rule as every lesson so far: the student listens **twice with no text**, then reads.
> Audio files: `01-passage.mp3` first, then the other parts in order. Part `05-would-and-if.mp3` is new — the contracted *'d* for *would* and *had*, and the weak *if*.

### 1.1 Before listening (2 minutes, Arabic is fine here)

1. If your connection failed in the middle of a class, what would you do?
2. What do you and your neighbours share, and what rules do you keep about it?
3. If you had one thing to make studying easier, what would you choose, and why?

### 1.4 Now read the passage

### Passage: *The Line We Share* (516 words)

The connection comes into the street on one line, and everything else hangs off it. From a box on the third floor it goes up to an antenna on the roof, across to a second antenna on the roof opposite, and from there into four more flats. Seven families, one uplink.

**[A]** A mesh works like that: every point relays the signal on to the next, so a street can share one line instead of buying seven. No single family here could afford the line on its own, and together they can. It is cheap and it is clever, and it has one weakness that everybody who uses it learns in the first week. If the uplink fails, nothing after it works. The antennas are all fine. There is simply nothing to pass on.

Aya has a class at eight on Monday evenings — thirty students, a teacher in another city, and a slide deck that has to load. If the line is slow, the video stops and the voice survives, which she can work with. If the line goes down, the lesson is over for all thirty of them, because nobody has a second way in.

**[B]** So she prepares for both evenings at once. She downloads the slides on Sunday night, when the line is quiet and the latency is low, and she keeps the last four weeks of recordings on the laptop. If the class fails on Monday, she will read the slides and send her questions as messages. If it does not fail, she has lost nothing but twenty minutes of a quiet Sunday.

The families have rules, which is what makes a shared line reliable at all. Nobody sends anything large between seven and ten. If somebody has to, they say so first. If two people ignore that on the same evening, everyone knows within a minute, because the latency climbs and every class in the street begins to stutter.

**[C]** Aya is careful about what she says she would do with a faster line, because a wish is an easy thing to turn into an excuse. If she had a reliable fifty megabits, she says, she would stop planning around the connection and spend that hour on the work itself. She would also stop apologising at the start of every call.

**[D]** There is an application open on the laptop that she has been filling in for three weeks: a university in Spain, an exchange place with a small scholarship attached, and a language requirement she is four months away from meeting. If she is accepted, she will go for one semester. If she is not, she will apply again in the spring. Either way the English has to be finished, so the English gets done. That part is hers, and it is the one part the line cannot reach.

The tower on the roof is a length of pipe, two brackets and a cable tie, and a neighbour put it up in an afternoon. If it comes down in the next storm, they will put it up again. They have done it twice.

### 1.5 Read aloud

Read the passage aloud **once** and record it. Watch the tune of the conditional sentences: the *if*-clause rises, the main clause falls. Read three of them aloud twice, listening for the shape rather than the words.

### 2.2 Synonyms and opposites

| Word | Synonym | Opposite |
|---|---|---|
| reliable | dependable, steady | unreliable |
| afford | be able to pay for | be too expensive for |
| apply | put in a request | withdraw |
| relay | pass on, forward | hold back |
| latency | delay, lag | an instant reply |
| requirement | condition, must-have | an option |
| share | use together | keep to yourself |
| fail | stop working | hold up |

### 2.3 Expressions to learn

| Expression | What it really means |
|---|---|
| **hangs off it** | depends completely on it |
| **a second way in** | another route to the same place when the first fails |
| **within a minute** | very quickly indeed |
| **either way** | whichever of the two things happens |
| **plan around something** | arrange everything else to fit a thing you cannot change |
| **turn a wish into an excuse** | use what you lack as a reason to stop trying |
| **four months away from** | needing four more months to reach |

parts.title: Grammar — the first and second conditional
parts.markdown:
### Come back to: the future with *will* and *going to*

Lesson 6 taught the two futures: **going to** for a decision already made,
**will** for a decision made as you speak, and for an opinion. Two lines to
remind you:

| She **is going to** apply in the spring. | it is decided |
|---|---|
| I think she **will** get in. | it is an opinion |

**New this time: after *when*, *as soon as*, *before*, *after* and *until*,
English uses the present simple for future time.**

This is the rule that the whole of today's grammar rests on, so it comes first:

- *I will send it **when the power comes** on.* ✓
- *I will send it when the power **will** come on.* ✗
- *She will apply again **after she finishes** the course.* ✓
- *Wait **until the latency drops**, and then upload it.* ✓

The future is already marked once, in the main clause, by *will*. English does
not mark it twice. The time clause looks present and means future.

| Time clause — present simple | Main clause — *will* |
|---|---|
| When the class **starts**, | she **will** turn the video off. |
| As soon as the uplink **comes** back, | the lesson **will** continue. |
| Before she **sends** anything large, | she **will** tell the others. |
| Until the storm **passes**, | nobody **will** climb to the roof. |

**Quick practice.** Put the verb in the right form.

1. I will call you when the power \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (come) on.
2. She will apply again after she \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (finish) the exam.
3. We will wait until the latency \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (drop).
4. As soon as the slides \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (load), the class \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (begin).

---

A **conditional** sentence has two halves: the *if*-clause, which sets a
condition, and the main clause, which says what follows. The order does not
matter — *If the uplink fails, nothing works* and *Nothing works if the uplink
fails* are the same sentence. **Put a comma in only when the *if*-clause comes
first.**

Today there are two of them, and the difference between them is not time. It is
**how likely the speaker thinks it is**.

### 3.1 The first conditional: real, and possible

**if + present simple , will + verb**

Use it for a real possibility in the future — something that may well happen:

| *If*-clause | Main clause |
|---|---|
| If the class **fails** on Monday, | she **will read** the slides. |
| If she **is** accepted, | she **will go** for one semester. |
| If it **comes** down in the storm, | they **will put** it up again. |

Notice that the *if*-clause follows exactly the rule you have just revised: it
is present in form and future in meaning. *If the uplink **will** fail* is
wrong for the same reason *when the power will come on* is wrong.

**You can replace *will* with another modal** when the meaning needs it:

- *If the line is slow, the video **may** stop.*
- *If you need to send something large, you **should** say so first.*
- *If the latency drops, we **can** start.*

### 3.2 The second conditional: unreal, or unlikely

**if + past simple , would + verb**

Use it for something that is **not true now**, or that you think will not
happen. The past tense here is not past time — it is distance from reality:

| *If*-clause | Main clause |
|---|---|
| If she **had** a reliable fifty megabits, | she **would stop** planning around it. |
| If I **lived** nearer the college, | I **would walk**. |
| If they **knew** which hour it was, | they **would plan** the week properly. |

She does not have fifty megabits. That is the whole point of the sentence. The
past tense is what tells you so.

**With *be*, use *were* for every person** in careful written English:

- *If I **were** you, I would apply.*
- *If the line **were** faster, she would not need Sunday night.*

(*If I was you* is common in speech and is not wrong there. Write *were*.)

**would** becomes **could** for ability and **might** for a weaker guess:
*If she had the money, she **could** buy a better antenna.*

### 3.3 First or second? The test — and it is not about time

| | First | Second |
|---|---|---|
| The speaker thinks | it may well happen | it is not true, or will not happen |
| *If*-clause | present simple | past simple |
| Main clause | *will* | *would* |
| Example | *If she is accepted, she will go.* | *If she had a faster line, she would stop planning.* |

Both sentences above are about the future. The tense does not tell you *when*;
it tells you **how real the speaker thinks it is**. Applying is real — she has
sent the form. Fifty megabits is not.

### 3.4 *unless* = *if … not*

**unless** replaces an *if*-clause that is negative, and then the clause itself
turns positive:

| With *if … not* | With *unless* |
|---|---|
| *If the uplink **does not** come back, the class is over.* | ***Unless** the uplink comes back, the class is over.* |
| *If you **do not** tell them first, they will be annoyed.* | ***Unless** you tell them first, they will be annoyed.* |

Two negatives is the mistake to watch for: *unless the uplink does not come
back* says the opposite of what you mean.

### 3.5 Negative and question

| | First | Second |
|---|---|---|
| Negative | If it **does not** load, she **will not** wait. | If she **did not** have the recordings, she **would not** cope. |
| Question | **What will** you do if it fails? | **What would** you do if you had a faster line? |

### 3.6 Grammar practice

**A. First conditional. Put both verbs in the right form:**

1. If the uplink \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (fail), the class \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (be) over.
2. If she \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (be) accepted, she \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (go) for one semester.
3. If two people \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (ignore) the rule, everyone \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (know).
4. She \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (send) her questions as messages if the lesson \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (not happen).

**B. Second conditional. Put both verbs in the right form:**

1. If she \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (have) a faster line, she \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (stop) planning around it.
2. If I \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (be) you, I \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (apply) this year.
3. If they \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (know) when the power was coming, they \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (not need) a plan.
4. What \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ you \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (do) if the tower \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (come) down tonight?

**C. First or second? Choose, and say why:**

1. If it rains tomorrow, we (will stay / would stay) inside.
2. If I (am / were) rich, I (will buy / would buy) everyone a line.
3. If the slides (load / loaded) in time, the class (will start / would start) at eight.
4. If she (does not get / did not get) the place, she (will apply / would apply) again.

**D. Rewrite with *unless*:**

1. If the uplink does not come back, the class is over.
2. If you do not tell them first, they will be annoyed.

**E. Come back to — *when*, *before*, *until*:**

1. I will upload it when the latency \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (drop).
2. She will not apply until she \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (pass) the exam.
3. Before she \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ (send) anything large, she will tell the others.

parts.title: The contracted 'd, and the weak if-clause
parts.markdown: ### 3.7 The contracted *'d*, and the weak *if*-clause (listen to `05-would-and-if.mp3`) The second conditional has two words doing all the work — *if* and *would* — and in speech both of them nearly disappear. **1. *would* becomes *'d*, which is one sound: /d/.** | Written in full | What you hear | |---|---| | I would stop. | /aɪd ˈstɒp/ | | She would go. | /ʃid ˈɡəʊ/ | | They would put it up again. | /ðeɪd ˈpʊt ɪt ʌp əˈɡen/ | | We would not wait. | /wi ˈwʊdnt ˈweɪt/ | Note the last line: the **negative keeps its full form**, *wouldn't* /ˈwʊdnt/. As with *can* and *can't*, the negative is the loud one. **2. *'d* is also *had*. The verb after it tells you which.** This is the one that confuses people, and the rule is simple: | You hear | Next word is | So *'d* means | Full sentence | |---|---|---|---| | /ʃid ˈɡəʊ/ | *go* — a bare verb | **would** | She **would** go. | | /ʃid ˈɡɒn/ | *gone* — a past participle | **had** | She **had** gone. | **'d + bare verb = would. 'd + past participle = had.** Nothing else can happen, so the verb after it always decides. **3. The *if*-clause is weak and runs together.** *If* is almost never stressed. It reduces to /əf/ and glues itself to what follows: | Written | What you actually hear | |---|---| | If I had a faster line | /əf aɪ ˈhæd ə ˈfɑːstə ˈlaɪn/ | | If she is accepted | /əf ʃiz əkˈseptɪd/ | | If it comes down | /əf ɪt ˈkʌmz ˈdaʊn/ | And the whole *if*-clause is said on a **rising tone**, which is what tells the listener that the sentence has not finished yet. The main clause falls. Copy the tune, not only the words: if you let the *if*-clause fall, people will think you have stopped speaking and will answer you. In the audio you hear each line twice, and then a test: say whether the *'d* you hear is **would** or **had**.

segments.say: Pronunciation. The contracted D, and the weak if clause.
First, would becomes a single D on the end of the pronoun. Listen to each line twice, then repeat it.
I'd stop.
I'd stop.
She'd go for one semester.
She'd go for one semester.
They'd put it up again.
They'd put it up again.
But the negative keeps its full form. Listen.
We wouldn't wait.
We wouldn't wait.
Now the hard part. That same D can be had. The verb after it tells you which. A bare verb means would. A past participle means had. Listen to the pair.
She'd go.
She'd gone.
The first was would go. The second was had gone.
Now the if clause. If is weak, and it runs into the words after it. The if clause rises, and the main clause falls. Listen to the tune, not only the words.
If I had a faster line, I'd stop planning around it.
If I had a faster line, I'd stop planning around it.
If she is accepted, she'll go in September.
If she is accepted, she'll go in September.
If it comes down, they'll put it up again.
If it comes down, they'll put it up again.
Now the test. You will hear a sentence with a D. Say whether the D is would, or had. Then you will hear the answer.
Sentence 1.
She'd apply again in the spring.
The answer is would.
Sentence 2.
She'd applied before the deadline.
The answer is had.
Sentence 3.
They'd finished by eight o'clock.
The answer is had.
Sentence 4.
They'd share the line with us.

parts.title: Writing — If the Connection Failed Tonight
parts.markdown:
### 5.2 Writing — "If the Connection Failed Tonight" (14–16 sentences)

**Model answer (copy the shape, change the words):**

> Our building shares one line with the two beside it, and everything we do depends on it. If the uplink fails, nobody has a second way in, so I have a plan for both kinds of evening. I download everything I will need on Sunday, when the latency is low and nobody is sending anything large. If my class goes down on Monday, I will read the slides I already have and send my questions as messages. If it does not go down, I have lost twenty quiet minutes and nothing else. We keep one rule in the group, and it is enough: tell the others before you send something big. If two people ignore it on the same night, everybody knows within a minute. People sometimes ask me what I would do with a faster connection. If I had one, I would stop planning around it and put that hour into the work itself, and I would stop apologising at the start of every call. If I were honest, though, the plan is not only about the line. I will keep making it after the line improves, because a week with a plan is steadier than a week without one. As soon as I pass the language test I will send the application, and if it is refused I will send it again in the spring.

**Checklist before you send it:**

- [ ] I used the **first conditional** at least **four** times, with *present simple + will*.
- [ ] I used the **second conditional** at least **twice**, with *past simple + would*.
- [ ] I used **if I were**, not *if I was*, in writing.
- [ ] I used **unless**, or *as soon as* / *when* with a present simple, at least once.
- [ ] I put a comma after the *if*-clause only when it came first.
- [ ] I used at least **5 new words** from Session 2.
- [ ] I used at least **2 words** from Lesson 6 or Lesson 7.
- [ ] My text has 14–16 sentences.

parts.title: Answer key and teacher notes
parts.markdown:
**Listening:** L1 — from a box on the third floor, up to an antenna on the roof and across to a second antenna on the roof opposite · L2 — the lesson is over for all thirty students, because nobody has a second way in · L3 — she downloads the slides, because the line is quiet and the latency is low · L4 — an exchange place at a university in Spain, with a small scholarship

**Part A (MCQ):** 1-C · 2-B · 3-D · 4-A · 5-C · 6-B · 7-B · 8-C · 9-C · 10-D

*Why 7 is **[B]***: the sentence weighs the cost of preparing against the benefit, and only the paragraph after **[B]** does that — Sunday's download, the kept recordings, and the closing line that she has lost nothing but twenty minutes of a quiet Sunday. The paragraph after **[A]** explains the mesh, after **[C]** is the faster line she does not have, after **[D]** the application.

*Why 8 is **C***: the paragraph opens by saying she is careful about the wish, because a wish is easy to turn into an excuse. The point is not the fifty megabits; it is the line she draws between what she cannot change and what she can.

*Why 9 is **C***: the technology is explained only as far as the story needs, the application is one paragraph of seven, and the rules about large uploads are reported, not argued for. The passage follows one person working around a shared constraint.

*Why 10 is **D, respectful***: **A is the trap.** *Pitying* would be a reasonable guess from the subject matter, and it is wrong — pity would dwell on what is missing. This writer dwells on what is done: the plan, the rules, the second antenna, the tower put up twice. The one sentence that could invite pity, about apologising at the start of every call, is given as something she intends to stop, not as something to feel sorry about. Attitude questions reward reading the **selection of detail**, not the subject.

**Part B (True/False):**

1. F — Seven families share one uplink through a mesh.
2. T
3. T
4. T
5. T
6. F — She will apply again in the spring.

**Part C (Fill in the blanks):** 1. uplink · 2. mesh · 3. tower · 4. latency · 5. reliable · 6. scholarship · 7. requirement
*(Extra words: antenna, relay)*

**2.4 A (Opposites):** 1. unreliable · 2. be too expensive for · 3. withdraw · 4. keep to yourself · 5. an instant reply

**2.4 B (Odd one out):** 1. scholarship (the others are on or above a building) · 2. requirement (the others are parts of a network) · 3. neighbour (the others are properties of a connection)

**Come back to (time clauses):** 1. comes · 2. finishes · 3. drops · 4. load … will begin

**3.6 A (first conditional):** 1. fails … will be · 2. is … will go · 3. ignore … will know · 4. will send … does not happen

**3.6 B (second conditional):** 1. had … would stop · 2. were … would apply · 3. knew … would not need · 4. would … do … came

**3.6 C (first or second, and why):**

1. will stay — rain tomorrow is a real possibility
2. were … would buy — she is not rich; the past tense marks it as unreal
3. load … will start — a real possibility this evening
4. does not get … will apply — she may well not get it; it is real either way

**3.6 D (*unless*):** 1. Unless the uplink comes back, the class is over. · 2. Unless you tell them first, they will be annoyed.

**3.6 E (time clauses):** 1. drops · 2. passes · 3. sends

**Mini-quiz:** 1. present simple, *will* · 2. past simple, *would* · 3. No — it means distance from reality: the thing is not true, or is not expected · 4. *if … not* · 5. the present simple · 6. *had*, because *gone* is a past participle; *'d* + bare verb is *would*, *'d* + past participle is *had* · 7. unreliable · 8. latency · 9–12. teacher judgement

### Teacher Notes {: #teacher-notes }

**What changed from Lesson 7, and what deliberately did not.** 516 words, against 510 in Lesson 7 and 504 in Lesson 6 — three lessons at one length, which was the point of the plateau. Over these three weeks the difficulty has moved entirely into the grammar and the vocabulary: the future, then the modals, now the conditionals, with the technical density climbing each time. The question set has not changed since Lesson 5 and will not change again.

**The one real difficulty.** Not the forms, which are two patterns on a card. It is understanding that **the past tense in the second conditional is not past time**. Arabic does not use a past form to mark unreality, so *if she had a faster line* reads to her as a sentence about last year. Section 3.3 is the one to work: both example sentences are about the future, and the only thing the tense tells you is how real the speaker thinks it is. Ask her, for each sentence in 3.6 C, *does the speaker think this will happen?* — the answer to that chooses the tense.

**The rule everything rests on.** The *Come back to* section is deliberately placed before the conditionals rather than after. *I will call you when the power comes on* and *if the power comes on, I will call you* are the same rule: the future is marked once, in the main clause, and the subordinate clause stays present. A student who has that rule finds the first conditional almost automatic; a student who has not will write *if the uplink will fail* for a year. Teach it first even if you run out of time for 3.5.

**Why the pronunciation part is the one to protect.** The whole second conditional hangs on one consonant, and that consonant is ambiguous: *'d* is *would* and *'d* is *had*. The test is mechanical — a bare verb after it means *would*, a past participle means *had* — and once she has it, a large amount of spoken English stops being a guess. The weak *if* and the rising tune matter nearly as much: if she lets the *if*-clause fall, people will answer before she has finished the sentence.

**Why this story, and a note on it.** The passage touches her own situation — a shared line, a class that depends on it, an exchange application with a language requirement. That is on purpose, and so is the distance: the student in it is somebody else, the detail is practical rather than personal, and nothing in it is there to be felt sorry about. The conditionals need a real constraint to be about, because a conditional sentence is how a person reasons about what is and is not within reach, and that is exactly what this passage is doing.

**Success criteria for Lesson 8.** The student should be able to:

- answer L1–L4 correctly on the second hearing;
- hear *she'd gone* and *she'd go* and say which is which, and why;
- build both conditionals and choose between them for a reason she can state;
- use the present simple after *if*, *when*, *until*, *as soon as* and *before*;
- write *if I were*, not *if I was*;
- rewrite an *if … not* sentence with *unless*;
- use 10 of the 14 key words in her own sentence;
- write 14 sentences with fewer than 4 conditional errors.

**If it is too easy:** add the third conditional (*if she had applied, she would have gone*) and the mixed conditional, both of which follow naturally from the *'d* work in part 05.
**If it is too hard:** teach the first conditional alone this week, with the time-clause rule, and leave the second for a week of its own. The second conditional is the harder idea by a long way, and splitting them costs nothing.

**A note on spaced recall.** `03-vocabulary.mp3` ends with five Lesson 6 words — *download, cloud, schedule, laptop, socket*. Lesson 7 recalled Lesson 5, so the two-lesson gap holds. Lesson 7's words are due back in Lesson 9.

**Where the course is now.** Eight lessons, one progress test, a complete TOEFL question set and eight tenses or structures, all spiralled at least twice. The length has been flat for three lessons, which means the next decision is whether Lesson 9 lets it rise again or holds it a fourth time — that is a question about her, not about the material, and the self-report at 6.3 is where the answer should come from. A second progress test, covering Lessons 4 to 8, would fit naturally before Lesson 9.

segments.say: Slow version. The passage, read slowly, one time.

The connection comes into the street on one line, and everything else hangs off it. From a box on the third floor it goes up to an antenna on the roof, across to a second antenna on the roof opposite, and from there into four more flats. Seven families, one uplink.

A mesh works like that: every point relays the signal on to the next, so a street can share one line instead of buying seven. No single family here could afford the line on its own, and together they can. It is cheap and it is clever, and it has one weakness that everybody who uses it learns in the first week. If the uplink fails, nothing after it works. The antennas are all fine. There is simply nothing to pass on.

Aya has a class at eight on Monday evenings — thirty students, a teacher in another city, and a slide deck that has to load. If the line is slow, the video stops and the voice survives, which she can work with. If the line goes down, the lesson is over for all thirty of them, because nobody has a second way in.

So she prepares for both evenings at once. She downloads the slides on Sunday night, when the line is quiet and the latency is low, and she keeps the last four weeks of recordings on the laptop. If the class fails on Monday, she will read the slides and send her questions as messages. If it does not fail, she has lost nothing but twenty minutes of a quiet Sunday.

The families have rules, which is what makes a shared line reliable at all. Nobody sends anything large between seven and ten. If somebody has to, they say so first. If two people ignore that on the same evening, everyone knows within a minute, because the latency climbs and every class in the street begins to stutter.

Aya is careful about what she says she would do with a faster line, because a wish is an easy thing to turn into an excuse. If she had a reliable fifty megabits, she says, she would stop planning around the connection and spend that hour on the work itself. She would also stop apologising at the start of every call.

There is an application open on the laptop that she has been filling in for three weeks: a university in Spain, an exchange place with a small scholarship attached, and a language requirement she is four months away from meeting. If she is accepted, she will go for one semester. If she is not, she will apply again in the spring. Either way the English has to be finished, so the English gets done. That part is hers, and it is the one part the line cannot reach.

The tower on the roof is a length of pipe, two brackets and a cable tie, and a neighbour put it up in an afternoon. If it comes down in the next storm, they will put it up again. They have done it twice.
